title: Visual Pathway and Visual Field Defects

questions.sec: Visual pathway — fibre composition at each station
questions.q: In the book's visual-pathway scheme, visual impulses are generated by the retina and the image is finally perceived in the:
questions.exp: Retina generates visual impulses and the occipital cortex perceives the image; a lesion along the visual pathway produces a visual field defect. (Book p21)

questions.sec: Visual pathway — fibre composition at each station
questions.q: Match the visual field half with the retinal fibres that carry it — 1) Nasal visual field 2) Temporal visual field … A) Nasal fibres B) Temporal fibres
opts: Both are carried by nasal fibres
Both are carried by temporal fibres
questions.exp: The figure key: nasal visual field → temporal fibres; temporal visual field → nasal fibres. (Book p21)

questions.sec: Visual pathway — fibre composition at each station
questions.q: The optic nerve carries which fibre combination per the book?
opts: Ipsilateral temporal plus ipsilateral nasal fibres
Contralateral temporal plus ipsilateral nasal fibres
questions.exp: Optic nerve (ON): I/L temporal + I/L nasal fibres. (Book p21)

questions.sec: Visual pathway — fibre composition at each station
questions.q: At the optic chiasm the event printed in the book is:
opts: Decussation of half of the macular fibres only (macular)
Crossing of nasal fibres (chiasm holds B/L nasal)
Crossing over of temporal fibres (both eyes)
Relay of all fibres to the lateral geniculate body (LGB)
questions.exp: Optic chiasm (OC): crossing over of nasal fibres; it contains B/L nasal fibres. (Book p21)

questions.sec: Visual pathway — fibre composition at each station
questions.q: Match the post-chiasmal station with its fibre content — 1) Optic tract 2) Lateral geniculate body 3) Optic radiations … A) Ipsilateral temporal plus contralateral nasal fibres B) Relay centre for the same fibre set C) Same fibres en route to the visual cortex
questions.exp: Optic tract, LGB (the relay centre) and optic radiations all carry I/L temporal + C/L nasal fibres to the visual cortex. (Book p21)

questions.sec: Visual pathway — fibre composition at each station
questions.q: Fill up: at the optic chiasm the fibres that cross over are the ______ fibres, so the chiasm contains them from both eyes.
questions.exp: Optic chiasm: crossing over of nasal fibres; the chiasm therefore contains B/L nasal fibres while temporal fibres stay ipsilateral. (Book p21)

questions.sec: Visual pathway — fibre composition at each station
questions.q: Which statement about the book's pathway diagram is FALSE?
opts: The optic chiasm contains bilateral temporal fibres
A lesion anywhere along the pathway gives a visual field defect
The lateral geniculate body is labelled the relay centre
The optic radiations are drawn as superior and inferior fibres
questions.exp: The chiasm contains bilateral NASAL fibres (crossing nasal fibres), not temporal fibres; LGB is the relay centre and the radiations split into superior and inferior fibres. (Book p21)

questions.sec: Pre-chiasmal and chiasmal lesions (1-3)
questions.q: A left optic nerve lesion produces which field defect for the left-sided lesions described in the book?
questions.exp: Optic nerve lesion (I/L temporal + I/L nasal fibres) gives I/L anopia (blindness). (Book p22)

questions.sec: Pre-chiasmal and chiasmal lesions (1-3)
questions.q: The earliest visual field defect in any optic nerve disease per the book is:
questions.exp: Macular/central fibres in the ON are most susceptible to ischemia and are affected first, so the earliest field defect is an ipsilateral central scotoma. (Book p22)

questions.sec: Pre-chiasmal and chiasmal lesions (1-3)
questions.q: Match the chiasmal fibre group with its field defect — 1) Bilateral nasal fibres 2) Bilateral inferonasal fibres 3) Bilateral superonasal fibres … A) Bitemporal inferior quadrantanopia B) Bitemporal/heteronymous hemianopia C) Bitemporal superior quadrantanopia
questions.exp: Chiasmal lesions: B/L nasal → bitemporal/heteronymous hemianopia; B/L inferonasal → bitemporal inferior quadrantanopia; B/L superonasal → bitemporal superior quadrantanopia. (Book p22)

questions.sec: Pre-chiasmal and chiasmal lesions (1-3)
questions.q: Match the cause with its direction of pressure on the chiasm in the book's list — 1) Pituitary adenoma 2) Craniopharyngioma 3) Anterior communicating artery aneurysm … A) From Rathke's pouch, superiorly B) From the sella turcica, inferiorly C) Laterally/compressing the chiasm lying under the ACA
questions.exp: Causes of chiasmal compression: 3rd ventricular glioma; pituitary adenoma from the sella turcica inferiorly; craniopharyngioma from Rathke's pouch superiorly; ACA aneurysm; carotid sinus thrombosis laterally — the chiasm lies under the ACA. (Book p22)

questions.sec: Pre-chiasmal and chiasmal lesions (1-3)
questions.q: A 45-year-old with a pituitary adenoma compressing the chiasm from below undergoes perimetry early in the disease. The book's earliest expected defect is:
questions.exp: B/L inferonasal fibre involvement gives bitemporal inferior quadrantanopia, labelled the earliest VFD in pituitary adenoma (pressure from below). (Book p22)

questions.sec: Pre-chiasmal and chiasmal lesions (1-3)
questions.q: A child with a suprasellar mass arising from Rathke's pouch shows an early field defect. Per the book it is:
questions.exp: Craniopharyngioma (from Rathke's pouch, superiorly) involves B/L superonasal fibres first, giving bitemporal superior quadrantanopia — the earliest VFD in craniopharyngioma. (Book p22)

questions.sec: Pre-chiasmal and chiasmal lesions (1-3)
questions.q: Match the junctional (proximal optic nerve) lesion fibre set with its components — the anterior knee of Wilbrand lesion takes: 1) I/L temporal 2) I/L nasal 3) C/L inferonasal … producing the junctional scotoma. Which combination is printed?
questions.exp: Junction of ON and OC (proximal ON): anterior knee of Wilbrand lesion involves I/L temporal + I/L nasal + C/L inferonasal fibres, producing a junctional scotoma; cause: meningioma. (Book p22)

questions.sec: Pre-chiasmal and chiasmal lesions (1-3)
questions.q: The book gives which cause for a junctional scotoma?
questions.exp: Junctional scotoma (junction of ON and OC, anterior knee of Wilbrand) — cause: meningioma. (Book p22)

questions.sec: Post-chiasmal lesions (4-10) and lobe syndromes
questions.q: Bilateral temporal fibre involvement at the lateral optic chiasm produces:
questions.exp: Lateral optic chiasma (B/L temporal fibres) gives binasal hemianopia, noted as very rare. (Book p23)

questions.sec: Post-chiasmal lesions (4-10) and lobe syndromes
questions.q: Match the post-chiasmal station with the field defect of its lesion — 1) Optic tract (5) 2) LGB (6) 3) Optic radiations (7) … A) Contralateral homonymous hemianopsia for all three B) Only the tract gives a hemianopsia C) Only the radiations give a hemianopsia D) The LGB gives a quadrantanopia
questions.exp: Lesions at 5 (OT), 6 (LGB) and 7 (OR) all involve I/L temporal + C/L nasal fibres and give C/L homonymous hemianopsia. (Book p23)

questions.sec: Post-chiasmal lesions (4-10) and lobe syndromes
questions.q: Meyer's loop is which part of the optic radiations, and its lesion gives:
opts: Inferior optic radiations — contralateral homonymous inferior quadrantanopia (pie on the floor)
Inferior optic radiations — pie in the sky (temporal)
Superior optic radiations — contralateral homonymous superior quadrantanopia (pie in the sky)
questions.exp: Superior OR (Meyer's loop) carries superior I/L temporal + C/L nasal fibres; its lesion gives C/L homonymous superior quadrantanopia, AKA pie in the sky. (Book p23)

questions.sec: Post-chiasmal lesions (4-10) and lobe syndromes
questions.q: The book's mnemonic TIPS stands for:
opts: Tract inferior pie on the floor
Temporal inferior pie in the sky
questions.exp: Mnemonic TIPS = Temporal Inferior Pie in the Sky, for Meyer's loop (temporal lobe) lesions. (Book p23)

questions.sec: Post-chiasmal lesions (4-10) and lobe syndromes
questions.q: Temporal lobe disease features listed with Meyer's loop lesions include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Temporal lobe disease features: uncinate fits, seizures, visual hallucinations; agraphia belongs to the parietal lobe list. (Book p23)

questions.sec: Post-chiasmal lesions (4-10) and lobe syndromes
questions.q: Baum's loop is which part of the radiations, and its lesion gives:
opts: Inferior radiations — pie on the floor
Superior optic radiations — pie in the sky (temporal loop)
questions.exp: Inferior OR (Baum's loop) carries inferior I/L temporal + C/L nasal fibres; its lesion gives C/L homonymous inferior quadrantanopia, AKA pie on the floor. (Book p23)

questions.sec: Post-chiasmal lesions (4-10) and lobe syndromes
questions.q: Parietal lobe disease features listed with Baum's loop lesions include all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Apraxia if the non-dominant lobe is involved
questions.exp: Parietal lobe disease features: aphasia, acalculia, agraphia, apraxia (non-dominant lobe); uncinate fits belong to the temporal lobe list. (Book p23)

questions.sec: Post-chiasmal lesions (4-10) and lobe syndromes
questions.q: A lesion of the tip of the occipital cortex (macular representation) produces:
opts: Contralateral homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing (sparing)
questions.exp: 10a) Tip of cortex lesion (macular representation) gives C/L homonymous macular defect, AKA cookie centre defect. (Book p23)

questions.sec: Post-chiasmal lesions (4-10) and lobe syndromes
questions.q: Which statement about occipital lobe lesions is FALSE per the book?
opts: A complete occipital lobe lesion gives macular sparing
A lesion of the visual cortex except its tip spares the macular representation
Cortical lesions except the tip give C/L homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing
A complete occipital lobe lesion gives C/L homonymous hemianopia and is rare
questions.exp: Complete occipital lobe lesion leads to C/L homonymous hemianopia (no sparing) and is rare; macular sparing belongs to cortex-except-tip lesions. (Book p23)

questions.sec: Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
questions.q: The abnormal pupil seen with an optic tract lesion is named:
questions.exp: In the OT/LGB/OR comparison table the pupil is abnormal in OT lesions — Wernicke's pupil — and normal in LGB and OR lesions. (Book p24)

questions.sec: Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
questions.q: Match the lesion site with the optic atrophy pattern — 1) Optic tract 2) LGB 3) Optic radiations … A) Present (+) B) Absent because the optic radiations are post-ganglionic C) Present bilaterally — I/L superior and inferior, C/L bow-tie pattern
questions.exp: Optic atrophy: OT — present bilaterally (I/L superior and inferior, C/L bow-tie pattern); LGB — present (+); OR — absent because optic radiations are post-ganglionic. (Book p24)

questions.sec: Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
questions.q: Which statement about congruity of the visual loss is FALSE per the book's table?
opts: Optic radiation lesions give congruous defects
Optic tract lesions give incongruous defects
questions.exp: Congruity of parameters of LOV: incongruous for OT and LGB, congruous for OR. (Book p24)

questions.sec: Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
questions.q: The book lists associations and causes of optic tract lesions. All of the following belong EXCEPT:
opts: TB/syphilitic meningitis and posterior cerebral artery aneurysm
questions.exp: OT lesions are associated with C/L hemiplegia and CN III palsy, caused by TB/syphilitic meningitis and posterior cerebral artery aneurysm; craniopharyngioma is listed under chiasmal causes. (Book p24)

questions.sec: Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
questions.q: The lateral geniculate body is composed of how many laminae, and where do contralateral fibres relay?
opts: Four laminae; C/L fibres relay into 1 and 2
Six laminae; C/L fibres relay into 2, 3 and 5
Three laminae; C/L fibres relay into all
questions.exp: LGB is composed of 6 laminae: C/L fibres relay into 1, 4, 6 laminae and I/L fibres into 2, 3, 5 laminae. (Book p24)

questions.sec: Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
questions.q: Fill up: within the six laminae of the lateral geniculate body, ipsilateral fibres relay into laminae ______.
questions.exp: LGB laminae: C/L fibres relay into 1, 4, 6 laminae while I/L fibres relay into 2, 3, 5 laminae. (Book p24)

questions.sec: Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
questions.q: A keyhole visual field defect is caused by:
questions.exp: Miscellaneous lesions: keyhole VFD — cause: incomplete LGB lesion. (Book p24)

questions.sec: Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
questions.q: An altitudinal visual field defect is defined by respecting which boundary?
questions.exp: Altitudinal VFD respects the horizontal midline, appearing as B/L superior or B/L inferior loss. (Book p24)

questions.sec: Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
questions.q: The book's GOA mnemonic lists causes of altitudinal defects. All of the following belong EXCEPT:
questions.exp: GOA: Glaucoma, Optic disc Drusen, AION (anterior ischemic optic neuropathy); optic neuritis is listed under central scotoma causes. (Book p24)

questions.sec: Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
questions.q: The commonest cause behind optic-neuritis central scotoma in the book's list is:
questions.exp: Central scotoma causes include any ON lesion, e.g. optic neuritis with multiple sclerosis as the m/c cause; also toxic optic neuropathy/tobacco-alcohol amblyopia, hereditary optic neuropathy and cone dystrophy (Stargardt's disease). (Book p24)

questions.sec: Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
questions.q: All of the following are listed causes of central scotoma EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Central scotoma causes: any ON lesion (optic neuritis — MS m/c), toxic optic neuropathy/tobacco-alcohol amblyopia, hereditary optic neuropathy, cone dystrophy (Stargardt's disease); retinal detachment is not listed. (Book p24)

questions.sec: Cortical blindness and the visual evoked potential
questions.q: Cortical blindness results from a lesion in:
questions.exp: Cortical blindness: lesion in bilateral cortical hemisphere. (Book p25)

questions.sec: Cortical blindness and the visual evoked potential
questions.q: Denial of blindness by a cortically blind patient is named:
questions.exp: Anton's syndrome: patient in denial of blindness. (Book p25)

questions.sec: Cortical blindness and the visual evoked potential
questions.q: Statokinetic dissociation in cortical blindness is called:
questions.exp: Riddoch phenomenon: statokinetic disassociation. (Book p25)

questions.sec: Cortical blindness and the visual evoked potential
questions.q: Which statement about cortical blindness is FALSE per the book?
opts: The light reflex is lost with nerve damage
The pupils remain normal in cortical blindness
There is bilateral blindness of both eyes
questions.exp: In cortical blindness the pupil remains normal (the reflex arc is pre-cortical) while VEP is absent; bilateral blindness with Anton's and Riddoch phenomena completes the picture. (Book p25)

questions.sec: Cortical blindness and the visual evoked potential
questions.q: The investigation that differentiates functional from organic blindness in the book is:
questions.exp: VEP is absent in cortical blindness and differentiates functional from organic blindness. (Book p25)

questions.sec: Cortical blindness and the visual evoked potential
questions.q: A young woman claims total blindness after a stressful event; examination is unremarkable and the book's malingering/hysterical-blindness workup is planned. The expected VEP is:
opts: Absent in the claimed eye only
questions.exp: Other uses of VEP: malingering and hysterical blindness show a normal VEP. (Book p25)

questions.sec: Cortical blindness and the visual evoked potential
questions.q: All of the following are clinical features of cortical blindness in the book EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Clinical features: B/L blindness, Anton's syndrome, Riddoch phenomenon, and a pupil that remains normal. (Book p25)

units.title: The visual pathway — which fibres travel at each station
units.guide: The retina generates visual impulses and the occipital cortex perceives the image; any lesion in between yields a visual field defect. Field-fibre mapping: nasal visual field → temporal fibres, temporal visual field → nasal fibres. The optic nerve carries I/L temporal + I/L nasal fibres; the optic chiasm is where nasal fibres cross, so it contains B/L nasal fibres; optic tract, LGB (the relay centre) and optic radiations (superior and inferior fibres) all carry I/L temporal + C/L nasal fibres onward to the visual cortex.

units.title: Lesions 1-3 — optic nerve, optic chiasm and the junctional scotoma
units.guide: All features are described for left-sided lesions. Optic nerve (I/L temporal + I/L nasal) → I/L anopia; macular/central fibres are most susceptible to ischemia and fail first, so the earliest defect is an ipsilateral central scotoma. Chiasmal: B/L nasal → bitemporal/heteronymous hemianopia (causes: 3rd ventricular glioma, pituitary adenoma from the sella inferiorly, craniopharyngioma from Rathke's pouch superiorly, ACA aneurysm with the chiasm under the ACA, carotid sinus thrombosis laterally); B/L inferonasal → bitemporal inferior quadrantanopia (earliest in pituitary adenoma); B/L superonasal → bitemporal superior quadrantanopia (earliest in craniopharyngioma). Junction of ON and OC (proximal ON, anterior knee of Wilbrand): I/L temporal + I/L nasal + C/L inferonasal → junctional scotoma, caused by meningioma.

units.title: Lesions 4-10 — lateral chiasm, tract/LGB/radiations, loops and the occipital cortex
units.guide: Lateral chiasma (B/L temporal) → binasal hemianopia, very rare. Lesions 5 (OT), 6 (LGB), 7 (OR) → C/L homonymous hemianopsia. Superior OR (Meyer's loop) → C/L homonymous superior quadrantanopia, 'pie in the sky', mnemonic TIPS (Temporal Inferior Pie in the Sky), with temporal lobe features (uncinate fits, seizures, visual hallucinations). Inferior OR (Baum's loop) → C/L homonymous inferior quadrantanopia, 'pie on the floor', with parietal features (aphasia, acalculia, agraphia, apraxia if non-dominant). Occipital tip (macular representation) → C/L homonymous macular defect, 'cookie centre'; visual cortex except tip → C/L homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing; a complete occipital lesion gives C/L homonymous hemianopia and is rare.

units.title: Comparing tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
units.guide: OT/LGB/OR comparison: pupil abnormal (Wernicke's pupil) only in OT lesions; optic atrophy present bilaterally in OT (I/L superior and inferior, C/L bow-tie), present (+) in LGB, absent in OR (radiations are post-ganglionic); congruity incongruous for OT and LGB but congruous for OR; OT lesions associate with C/L hemiplegia and CN III palsy, caused by TB/syphilitic meningitis and PCA aneurysm; the LGB has 6 laminae — C/L fibres relay into 1, 4, 6 and I/L into 2, 3, 5. Miscellaneous: keyhole VFD from an incomplete LGB lesion; altitudinal VFD respects the horizontal midline (GOA — glaucoma, optic disc drusen, AION); central scotoma from any ON lesion (optic neuritis, MS m/c), toxic optic neuropathy/tobacco-alcohol amblyopia, hereditary optic neuropathy and cone dystrophy (Stargardt's).

units.title: Cortical blindness and the visual evoked potential
units.guide: Cortical blindness follows bilateral cortical hemisphere lesions: B/L blindness, Anton's syndrome (denial of blindness), Riddoch phenomenon (statokinetic dissociation) and a pupil that remains normal. VEP is absent and separates functional from organic blindness; malingering and hysterical blindness instead show a normal VEP.
